claims.claim_text: Wallach documents that specific mineral deficiencies produced specific deficiency diseases in distinct geographic regions — each disease appeared wherever the local soil lacked that mineral. His examples: iodine deficiency caused goiter (a swollen thyroid) in communities far from the sea; selenium deficiency caused Keshan disease, a cardiomyopathy (disease of the heart muscle), in Keshan Province, China; phosphate deficiency caused pica (a compulsive craving to eat non-food substances) in South Africa; and copper deficiency caused enzootic ataxia (a copper-deficiency disorder of movement and coordination) in Australia. In his words: "Iodine deficiency (goiter) occurred in communities living at a distance from the sea; Keshan disease (cardiomyopathy) caused by a selenium deficiency occurred in Keshan Province, China; phosphate deficiency (pica) was common in South Africa; copper deficiency (enzootic ataxia) was common in Australia, etc."
claims.verbatim:
Iodine deficiency (goiter) occurred in
communities living at a distance from the sea; Keshan disease
(cardiomyopathy) caused by a selenium deficiency occurred
in Keshan Province, China; phosphate deficiency (pica) was
common in South Africa; copper deficiency (enzootic ataxia)
was common in Australia, etc.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's health framework is built on an unusually large base of comparative pathology. As a pathologist for a multi-institution research program - The Center for the Biology of Natural Systems, funded by the U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH) along with several zoos and universities - he performed autopsies on a scale almost no one else has: more than 20,000 of them, spanning over 17,500 captive wild, laboratory, and domestic animals across more than 454 species, plus 3,000 humans for comparison. That vast cross-species record is what led him to his central claim - that creatures dying of so-called "natural causes" were really dying of nutritional deficiency diseases. In his words: "As a comparative pathologist, I (Wallach) performed more than 20,000 autopsies of over 17,500 captive wild animals, laboratory species and domestic animals, of over 454 species and 3,000 humans for a comparison."
claims.verbatim:
As a comparative pathologist, I (Wallach) performed
more than 20,000 autopsies of over 17,500 captive wild
animals, laboratory species and domestic animals, of over 454
species and 3,000 humans for a comparison.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's stance on carbohydrates and sugars: they are not essential nutrients. His reasoning is that the body can make all the carbohydrate and sugar it needs - for energy, upkeep, and structural repair - by breaking down and rebuilding fats and proteins inside the cell, so none has to come from the diet. This runs counter to the popular view of carbohydrates as a required food group. In his words: "Contrary to popular belief, carbohydrates and sugars are not essential nutrients by anybody's standards, as we can make all of the carbohydrates and sugars we need for energy and maintenance and repair of structural components by breaking down and reconfiguring fats and proteins at the cellular level."
claims.verbatim:
Contrary to popular belief, carbohydrates and sugars
are not essential nutrients by anybody’s standards, as we
can make all of the carbohydrates and sugars we need for
energy and maintenance and repair of structural components
by breaking down and reconfiguring fats and proteins at the
cellular level.

claims.claim_text: Wallach counts 12 essential amino acids - the protein building blocks the body cannot make for itself and so must obtain from food: valine, tyrosine, tryptophan, lysine, isoleucine, threonine, methionine, histidine, phenylalanine, arginine, taurine, and leucine. (Mainstream nutrition usually lists nine; Wallach's list adds tyrosine, arginine, taurine, and histidine.) He warns that if any essential amino acid is missing from the diet for any length of time, a specific - sometimes reversible - deficiency disease results. A footnote adds that selenium researcher Dr. Gerhard Schrauzer considered selenomethionine (the selenium form of methionine) a 13th essential amino acid. In his words: "There are 12 amino acids that are required by the body as protein building blocks, and because the body is unable to manufacture them, they are termed 'essential amino acids.'"
claims.verbatim:
There are 12 amino acids that are required by the body
as protein building blocks, and because the body is unable to
manufacture them, they are termed “essential amino acids.”

claims.claim_text: For more than 65 years it was known that omega-3 essential fatty acids were needed to prevent disease - but because the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) had ruled the evidence "inconclusive," it was actually illegal to tell people that omega-3 supplements could lower their risk of stroke and sudden cardiac death. Wallach fought this: his company (Wellness Lifestyles, Inc.) petitioned the FDA for a qualified health claim, and after a hard-fought battle, won - on September 8, 2004 the FDA allowed the claim linking omega-3 fatty acids to reduced coronary heart disease risk (Docket No. 03Q-0401). In his words: "To make a long story short, Wellness Lifestyles, Inc (Wallach) filed a petition for an Amended Health Claim: Omega-3 Fatty Acids and Coronary Heart Disease (Co-Petitioner); Docket No. 03Q-0401; filed on 6/23/2003; qualified claim allowed by FDA on 9/8/2004."
claims.verbatim:
To make a long story short, Wellness Lifestyles,
Inc (Wallach) filed a petition for an Amended Health
Claim: Omega-3 Fatty Acids and Coronary Heart Disease
(Co-Petitioner); Docket No. 03Q-0401; filed on 6/23/2003;
qualified claim allowed by FDA on 9/8/2004.

claims.claim_text: Is cholesterol bad for you? Wallach's answer is no - he calls it an essential nutrient. He points out that cholesterol is a necessary building block of the structural membranes of every cell, of all steroid hormones, and of the brain's myelin (the fatty insulating sheath around nerves) and nerve cells themselves. This counters the popular view of cholesterol as merely something to avoid. In his words: "Cholesterol is an essential nutrient and an essential component of the structural membranes of all cells, all steroid hormones and is a major component of brain (myelin) and nerve cells."
claims.verbatim:
Cholesterol is an essential nutrient and an essential
component of the structural membranes of all cells, all steroid
hormones and is a major component of brain (myelin) and
nerve cells.

claims.claim_text: Wallach warns that vitamin deficiencies during pregnancy can cause catastrophic birth defects - he lists neural tube defects, intellectual disability, muscular dystrophy, cystic fibrosis, cleft lip, cleft palate, and heart defects among the possible outcomes. This is a general warning; the specific nutrient-to-defect links (such as folic acid and neural tube defects, or zinc and cleft palate) are covered as their own operational claims. In his words: "Deficiencies of many vitamins during pregnancy can result in catastrophic birth defects (neural tube defects, mental retardation, muscular dystrophy, cystic fibrosis, cleft lip, cleft palate, heart defects, etc.)."
claims.verbatim:
Deficiencies of many vitamins during pregnancy
can result in catastrophic birth defects (neural tube defects,
mental retardation, muscular dystrophy, cystic fibrosis, cleft
lip, cleft palate, heart defects, etc.).

claims.claim_text: Wallach attributes the "morning sickness" of early pregnancy to a deficiency of vitamin B6 (pyridoxine): he notes it is commonly seen in the first trimester and is thought to be caused by too little B6. This complements his morning-sickness protocol elsewhere, which treats it with B6 plus a B-complex. In his words: '"Morning sickness" commonly observed in the first trimester of pregnancy is thought to be due to pyridoxine deficiency.'
claims.verbatim:
“Morning sickness” commonly observed in the first
trimester of pregnancy is thought to be due to pyridoxine
deficiency.

claims.claim_text: Does the birth-control pill deplete a nutrient? Per Wallach, yes: 15 to 20 percent of women taking oral contraceptives show symptoms of vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency - including malaise, depression, and glucose intolerance (trouble regulating blood sugar). In his words: "Fifteen to 20 percent of women taking oral contraceptives show the symptoms of pyridoxine deficiency manifested by malaise, depression and glucose intolerance."
claims.verbatim:
Fifteen to 20 percent of women taking oral contraceptives
show the symptoms of pyridoxine deficiency manifested by
malaise, depression and glucose intolerance.
